These things I have spoken to you that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
family.context: Jesus roots obedience in already-given love. The Father loves the Son; the Son loves his people the same way. Staying in that love produces joy, and joy overflows as mutual love that mirrors his. Joy here is not hype; it is Jesus’ own joy shared with those who stay in his love. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus loves us with the same steadfast love the Father has for him—secure, not fragile. Our love for one another is not invented from thin air; it is a response patterned after how he has already loved us, even to the cross. Commandment-keeping, in this frame, is relational loyalty to the One who loved first—patterned after the Son’s obedience to the Father. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Practice love “as I have loved you”: patient listening, covering an offense without keeping score, serving without announcing it. Let joy, not guilt, set the mood of obedience tonight. Let the discussion stay warm. Love as he loved is learned in tone as much as in tasks. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: Where have we felt Jesus’ love recently, and how could that shape how we treat each other this weekend?
family.prayer: Jesus, thank you for loving us as the Father loves you. Keep us in your love. Fill our home with your joy, and teach us to love one another as you have loved us. Amen.

devo.title: Return, Rebuild, and the Word Restored
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Ezra 1:1–4 — The LORD stirs Cyrus to send the exiles home
  2. Ezra 3:10–13 — The foundation laid: shouts of joy and weeping
  3. Ezra 7:6–10 — Ezra set his heart to study, do, and teach the law
  4. Ezra 9:5–9 — Ezra’s prayer: “a little reviving in our bondage”

New Testament fulfillment: Ephesians 2:19–22; Hebrews 8:1–2

The Book and Its Themes

Ezra tells of two returns from Babylonian exile. The first was under Zerubbabel and Jeshua (chapters 1–6). They rebuilt the altar and the temple despite opposition, finishing in 516 BC with the encouragement of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah (5:1). The second, about sixty years later, was under Ezra the priest and scribe (chapters 7–10), who led a reformation centered on God’s word. The themes are God’s sovereignty over kings (1:1), the rebuilding of worship, mixed joy and grief (3:12–13), opposition to God’s work, the centrality of Scripture, and repentance over compromise with the nations’ idolatry (chapters 9–10).

Where Ezra Stands in the Covenant Story

God had promised through Jeremiah that the exile would last seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10). Ezra 1:1 says the return happened “that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled” (KJV). The covenant God kept his word. But the return was humble. The old men who remembered Solomon’s temple wept (3:12), and the people were still “servants” under Persian rule (9:9). The post-exilic books show that the return from Babylon was real but not yet the full restoration the prophets promised. They teach Israel, and us, to keep waiting for the Messiah and the new covenant.

The issue of mixed marriages in Ezra 9–10 should be read in context. The concern was not ethnicity. Ruth the Moabite was honored. The concern was idolatry, and marriages that would pull Israel back to the “abominations” that had caused the exile (9:1, 11–14). The New Testament carries the principle forward as marrying “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39).

How Ezra Leads Us to Christ

  • Thematic fulfillment of the temple: The second temple was smaller and lacked the ark and the glory cloud. Haggai promised that the “latter glory” of this house would surpass the former (Haggai 2:9). That promise was fulfilled when the Lord himself came to his temple in the person of Jesus (Malachi 3:1; Luke 2:27–32). Through Christ, believers are built together into “an holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21).
  • Typology of priest and teacher: Ezra was both priest and scribe. He studied, obeyed, and taught God’s law (7:10), and he interceded for the people with confession as if their sin were his own (9:6). Jesus is the great High Priest who serves in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1–2) and the Teacher who speaks with authority (Matthew 7:29). Unlike Ezra, he did not need to confess his own sin. He bore ours.
  • Thematic analogy: Ezra’s “little reviving in our bondage” (9:8) anticipates the full liberation that Jesus announces (Luke 4:18; John 8:36).

Through Reformed Eyes

Ezra 7:10, “to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach” (KJV), is a model the Reformed tradition has loved. It joins knowledge, obedience, and teaching. It also corresponds roughly to John Frame’s three perspectives: the normative (God’s word), the existential (a heart set on it), and the situational (teaching it in a real community). The Reformation itself was in many ways an Ezra-like recovery of Scripture, read and preached to God’s people. Calvin’s practice of expository preaching through whole books is one expression of that.

For Today

Small beginnings can make us weep for what used to be or for what we hoped would be. But God was keeping his word in the day of small things (Zechariah 4:10). Set your heart today, like Ezra, to study God’s word, to do it, and to share it. And rejoice: you are being built into a temple greater than Solomon’s, because Christ is its cornerstone.

Reflect

  1. Which of Ezra’s three habits, studying, doing, or teaching, is weakest in your life right now?
  2. Where are you discouraged by “small beginnings,” and how does God’s faithfulness to Jeremiah’s word encourage you?

Pray

Faithful God, you stir the hearts of kings to fulfill your word. Thank you for bringing your people home and for Jesus, the true temple and the great High Priest. Set my heart to seek your law, to do it, and to teach it. Grant me reviving in my bondage. Build me with your people into a dwelling place for your Spirit. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.”
family.context: Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount by blessing people the world rarely applauds: the spiritually needy, the grieving, the gentle, those aching for what is right. The kingdom begins with empty hands, not impressive résumés. Jesus blesses hunger, not self-sufficiency. That alone overturns many family myths about strength. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus himself lived this way—meek, mourning over sin, hungry for the Father’s will—and he fulfills righteousness for us. In him, poverty of spirit is not despair; it is the doorway into his kingdom grace. He comforts mourners because he is the Man of Sorrows who also rose; kingdom comfort is personal. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Tonight, resist the urge to impress God or each other. Admit one need honestly. Families that can say “we need Jesus” stay soft enough for his blessing to land. Admitting need together can be the most blessed moment of the week. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: Where do we feel spiritually “poor” or hungry right now, and how might that be a place Jesus wants to meet us?
family.prayer: Jesus, we come with empty hands. Comfort our mourning, teach us meekness, and satisfy our hunger for what is right in you. Amen.

devo.title: Building Walls, Hearing the Word, Longing for the City
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Nehemiah 1:4–11 — Nehemiah’s prayer of confession and covenant appeal
  2. Nehemiah 4:14–20 — “Remember the Lord… our God shall fight for us”
  3. Nehemiah 8:1–10 — The law read and explained: “the joy of the LORD is your strength”
  4. Nehemiah 9:32–38 — “We are servants this day”

New Testament fulfillment: Hebrews 11:10, 16; Revelation 21:2–4

The Book and Its Themes

Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, hears that Jerusalem’s walls lie in ruins. He weeps, prays, and then acts. In fifty-two days, despite mockery, threats, and internal injustice, the wall is rebuilt (6:15). The work is followed by a great public reading of the law under Ezra, covenant renewal, and reforms. The book’s themes are prayerful leadership, courage under opposition, combining prayer with practical wisdom (“we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch,” 4:9, KJV), justice for the poor (chapter 5), the joy of hearing God’s word explained (chapter 8), and the persistent backsliding of the people (chapter 13).

Where Nehemiah Stands in the Covenant Story

Nehemiah’s prayer is grounded in covenant promise. He reminds God of his word through Moses: if the scattered return to him, he will gather them (1:8–9; Deuteronomy 30:1–4). The great prayer of chapter 9 rehearses the whole covenant story, from creation, Abraham, exodus, Sinai, wilderness, land, and judges to exile. It confesses that God has been just and they have been wicked (9:33). Then the people sign a covenant to obey (9:38). Yet the book ends with the people breaking those very promises: Sabbath violation, mixed marriages, and neglect of the temple (chapter 13). The last word is Nehemiah’s prayer, “Remember me, O my God, for good” (13:31, KJV). The reforms were real, but they could not change hearts. Israel needed the new covenant.

How Nehemiah Leads Us to Christ

  • Thematic fulfillment (the city): The rebuilt walls protected a small, vulnerable city. Hebrews tells us that Abraham was looking for “a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (11:10, KJV). Revelation 21 shows the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven, its walls secure and gates never shut, with God dwelling among his people. Christ is building this city, and he is its temple and lamp (Revelation 21:22–23).
  • Typology of the intercessor and leader: Nehemiah left the king’s palace to identify with a broken people, prayed for them, confessing their sins as “we” (1:6), and labored to restore them. Christ left heavenly glory, became one with us (Philippians 2:5–8), bore our sins, and ever lives to intercede (Hebrews 7:25). Unlike Nehemiah, he not only builds walls but makes a new heart.
  • Law and gospel: The people wept when they heard the law (8:9). Then they were told to rejoice, eat, drink, and send portions to those with nothing, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (8:10). The law exposes sin. Grace gives joy. Nehemiah 13 shows that covenant vows made in our own strength fail. Only Christ’s obedience secures the covenant (Hebrews 8:6–13).

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed emphasis on the preached and explained Word comes straight from passages like Nehemiah 8:8: they “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (KJV). The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 155) calls the reading and especially the preaching of the Word an effectual means of converting and building up sinners. On the other hand, Nehemiah 9–10 shows the difference between covenant renewal as a human promise and covenant security grounded in God. Wayne Grudem’s account of the covenant of grace (Systematic Theology, ch. 25) stresses that we enter by faith and continue in obedience, but that the guarantee rests on Christ’s work.

For Today

Nehemiah teaches that prayer and work belong together. Pray, then set a watch. Pray, then pick up the trowel. Whatever broken wall God has laid on your heart, whether a family, a church, or a neighborhood, bring it to him and then labor in faith. And when the law makes you weep over your failure, hear the good news: the joy of the Lord is your strength.

Reflect

  1. What “broken wall” has God laid on your heart, and what is one practical step you can take after praying?
  2. Do you find joy, not only conviction, when you hear God’s word? What would help you receive both?

Pray

O Lord, great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, I confess my sins and the sins of your people. Thank you that Jesus, our greater Nehemiah, left glory to rebuild what we ruined, and lives to intercede for us. Give me courage to build and faith to fight in your strength. Let your joy be my strength. Bring me at last to the city whose builder and maker is God. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.”
family.context: Jesus tells his disciples they already are salt and light—not that they must invent a public brand. Salt preserves and seasons; light reveals. Hiding either wastes the gift. Salt that stays in the jar and light under a basket both fail their purpose. Jesus assumes his people will season and illuminate ordinary rooms. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the true light of the world (John 8:12). Our shining is borrowed brightness—good works that point past us to the Father. We do not shine to earn glory but because we belong to him who is light. Because he is the light, our works are meant to redirect glory to the Father, never to build a family brand of goodness. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Ask where your household’s “lamp” tends to go under a basket—kindness at home that never reaches a neighbor, faith that stays private out of fear. Choose one simple, visible good that quietly points to God this week. Keep the good deed small enough to finish and clear enough to be noticed without a speech. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What is one way our family could “give light to all in the house”—and beyond it—without showing off?
family.prayer: Father, thank you for Jesus, our light. Make us salty with grace and bright with good works that give you glory, not us. Amen.

devo.title: For Such a Time as This: The Hidden Hand of God
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Esther 3:8–11 — Haman’s plot to destroy the Jews
  2. Esther 4:12–17 — “Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
  3. Esther 6:1–11 — A sleepless king and a sudden reversal
  4. Esther 9:20–22 — Sorrow turned to joy: the feast of Purim

New Testament fulfillment: Romans 8:28–39; Hebrews 7:25

The Book and Its Themes

Esther is famous for never mentioning God’s name. Yet God is everywhere in the story. A Jewish orphan becomes queen of Persia. Her cousin Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king. Haman, an enemy of the Jews, obtains a royal decree to destroy them. Esther risks her life to intercede, and in a cascade of “coincidences,” such as a king’s sleepless night (6:1) and gallows built for Mordecai, everything is reversed. The Jews are delivered, and Purim is established to remember how “sorrow was turned to joy” (9:22). Themes include providence, reversal of fortunes, the courage to identify with God’s people at personal cost, and the preservation of the covenant line.

Where Esther Stands in the Covenant Story

Haman is called an “Agagite” (3:1), recalling Agag king of Amalek (1 Samuel 15). Mordecai is a Benjamite descended from Kish (2:5), Saul’s family. The ancient conflict between Amalek and Israel (Exodus 17:14–16) surfaces again. Behind Haman’s plot lies the old enmity of Genesis 3:15: the serpent’s seed against the woman’s seed. If the Jews had been destroyed, there would have been no Messiah. The covenant promise to Abraham (“I will… curse him that curseth thee,” Genesis 12:3, KJV) is quietly kept in Persia.

How Esther Leads Us to Christ

  • Thematic fulfillment (preservation of the promised seed): God preserves the people from whom the Messiah would come. That is the whole Old Testament’s thread.
  • Typology of the mediator: Esther goes uninvited before the king at the risk of death, “if I perish, I perish” (4:16), to plead for her people. Christ did not merely risk death. He died, and now he appears in the presence of God for us (Hebrews 9:24) and always lives to intercede (Hebrews 7:25). Esther needed the king to hold out his scepter. Christ, the King’s Son, opens access for us permanently.
  • Typology of reversal: Haman built a gallows for Mordecai and was hanged on it himself (7:10). At the cross the powers that sought to destroy Christ were themselves disarmed and shamed (Colossians 2:15). The greatest reversal in history came on the third day.
  • Caution against allegory: Esther is not a symbol of the church, nor is the king a symbol of God in every detail. The book’s own way of pointing to Christ is through providence, intercession, and the preservation of the covenant people.

Through Reformed Eyes

Esther is a favorite text for the Reformed doctrine of providence. God “doth uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all creatures, actions, and things, from the greatest even to the least” (WCF 5.1). John Frame’s “control” lordship attribute fits a story in which a king’s insomnia saves a nation. Calvin warned against both fatalism and the notion of fortune, teaching that believers can take comfort in a Father’s sure care (Institutes 1.16.2–3; 1.17.11). Romans 8:28 is the New Testament summary of Esther: all things work together for good to those who love God, who are called according to his purpose.

For Today

You may not see God’s name written across your circumstances today. That does not mean he is absent. Your placement in your work, your family, and your community is not an accident. Mordecai’s question is a question for you: who knows whether you have come to your position “for such a time as this”? Speak and act faithfully, even at a cost. Then rest. The King who was raised from the dead holds out the scepter of grace to you.

Reflect

  1. Where might God have placed you “for such a time as this,” and what costly faithfulness might that require?
  2. Can you trace God’s hidden hand in a past season that once seemed random?

Pray

Sovereign God, though your name is sometimes hidden from my sight, your hand is never absent. Thank you for preserving your people and bringing the promised Savior into the world. Thank you that Jesus intercedes for me always, and that I have access to you through him. Give me courage like Esther’s to stand with your people and speak for truth. Turn sorrow to joy. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment… So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.”
family.context: Jesus digs beneath the outward act of murder to the heart of contempt and unresolved anger. Worship that ignores a broken relationship is incomplete. He prioritizes reconciliation even over a religious gift already in hand. Jesus treats contempt as spiritually serious because it corrodes the image of God in our neighbor and hardens worship into theater. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the reconciler who makes peace by his blood (Colossians 1:20). He does not merely ban murder; he forms peacemakers who refuse to nurse contempt. Coming to him means letting him interrupt our worship until we seek peace. He is able to heal anger because he absorbed hostility at the cross without returning curse for curse. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: If someone in the room—or someone you will see soon—has something against you, do not wait for the “perfect moment.” Take a first step toward repair: an apology, a clarifying question, a softened tone. If reconciliation needs time, still take the first honest step tonight rather than waiting for perfect feelings. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: Is there a tension in our home or circle that Jesus would tell us to address before we move on tonight?
family.prayer: Jesus, you make peace by your cross. Soften angry hearts in us. Help us seek reconciliation quickly and honestly. Amen.

devo.title: I Know That My Redeemer Liveth
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Job 1:6–12, 20–22 — The heavenly council and Job’s worship in loss
  2. Job 19:23–27 — “I know that my redeemer liveth”
  3. Job 38:1–11 — The LORD answers from the whirlwind
  4. Job 42:1–10 — Job’s repentance, restoration, and intercession for his friends

New Testament fulfillment: James 5:10–11; 1 Timothy 2:5

The Book and Its Themes

Job is the Bible’s great wrestling match with innocent suffering. A blameless man (1:1) loses wealth, children, and health in a single sequence of disasters permitted by God and carried out by Satan. Three friends arrive and, after a week of wise silence, insist that suffering must be punishment for sin. Job protests his innocence, cries out to God, and longs for a hearing. Then the LORD speaks from the whirlwind. He does not give Job an explanation, but a revelation of his own wisdom and power over creation. Job repents of speaking beyond his knowledge, and God vindicates him over his friends (42:7). Themes include the sovereignty of God over evil without God being its author, the limits of human wisdom, the inadequacy of simple retribution theology, honest lament, and faith that holds on in the dark.

Where Job Stands in the Covenant Story

Job likely lived in the patriarchal period outside Israel, in the land of Uz. He reminds us that God’s grace was never confined by geography. Job longs for something the book cannot yet supply: an “umpire” (Job 9:33, ESV; KJV “daysman”) to stand between God and man, a “witness in heaven” and an advocate (16:19–21), and a living Redeemer (go’el) who will stand on the earth at the last (19:25). The Old Testament here is reaching for the Mediator of the covenant.

How Job Leads Us to Christ

  • Thematic fulfillment (the Mediator): Job’s cry for a daysman who could “lay his hand upon us both” (9:33, KJV) is answered in “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5, KJV). Christ is truly God and truly man, and he alone can lay a hand on both.
  • Redeemer and resurrection: The exact sense of 19:25–27 is debated by scholars. Still, the church has long read it, rightly in its canonical context, as hope for a living Redeemer and for seeing God “in my flesh.” That hope is fulfilled in the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). Handel’s Messiah sets these words to music beside 1 Corinthians 15.
  • Typology of the righteous sufferer: Job suffered though blameless, and he was misjudged by friends as a sinner. Christ suffered as the truly sinless one and “was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). The difference is that Job’s suffering was not substitutionary. Christ’s was.
  • Typology of the intercessor: In the end, Job prays for his friends, and God accepts them because of Job’s prayer (42:8–10). Christ’s intercession secures our acceptance (Romans 8:34).

Through Reformed Eyes

The opening chapters display what Reformed theology calls God’s sovereignty over evil. Satan can do nothing without God’s permission, and God’s purposes are good even when Satan’s are evil. The Westminster Confession says God’s providence extends even to sin, yet in such a way that “the sinfulness thereof proceedeth only from the creature” (WCF 5.4). John Frame’s Apologetics and his work on the problem of evil, as well as Grudem’s chapter on providence, emphasize that Scripture does not give us a full theodicy. It gives us a trustworthy God. Calvin preached 159 sermons on Job, a sign of how central the book was to Reformed pastoral care.

For Today

Job does not teach you to suppress lament. Job cried out honestly and was vindicated, while his tidy-answer friends were rebuked. Bring your raw questions to God. But Job also teaches you to bow before a wisdom greater than your own. You may not receive explanations, but you have something better than Job had: a Mediator who has suffered, who stands between you and God, and who lives to save.

Reflect

  1. In your own suffering, or in comforting others, are you more like Job’s friends (quick to explain) or like Job (honest in lament)?
  2. How does knowing that your Redeemer lives change the way you face loss today?

Pray

LORD of the whirlwind, your wisdom is beyond my searching, and your ways are higher than mine. I bring you my questions and my grief. Thank you that I know my Redeemer lives, the Mediator who lays his hand on both God and me. When I cannot trace your hand, help me trust your heart. Make me a patient comforter of those who suffer. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.”
family.context: Jesus overturns the instinct to reserve love for allies. He ties enemy-love to the Father’s generous character—sun and rain given without favoritism—and to the family resemblance of those who belong to him. Enemy-love is one of Jesus’ most distinctive teachings. It reveals the Father’s generous character more than our natural instincts ever will. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus practiced this to the end, praying for those who crucified him. Loving enemies is possible because we have first been loved as former rebels reconciled by his grace. We pray for opponents as children reflecting our Father. We can pray for difficult people because Jesus intercedes for us and has already loved us at our worst. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: “Enemy” at home may mean a difficult coworker, a harsh relative, or someone who embarrassed you. Pray for them by name tonight—not a performance, a release of bitterness into Jesus’ care. Keep the prayer short and sincere. Bitterness loosens when we place a name in the Father’s care. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: Who is hard for us to love right now, and what would praying for them sound like in one sentence?
family.prayer: Father, your sun rises on us by mercy. Through Jesus, teach us to love those who oppose us and to pray for them with honest hearts. Amen.

devo.title: The Songbook of the Messiah and His People
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Psalm 1 — The blessed man and the two ways
  2. Psalm 2 — The LORD’s Anointed King: “Thou art my Son”
  3. Psalm 22:1–18, 27–31 — “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
  4. Psalm 110 — Priest forever after the order of Melchizedek

New Testament fulfillment: Luke 24:44–47; Hebrews 1:5–13; Matthew 27:46

The Book and Its Themes

The Psalms are Israel’s prayer book and hymnbook, 150 poems collected over about a thousand years in five books (1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150), each ending in a doxology. They include praise, thanksgiving, lament (the largest category), confession, wisdom, royal psalms, and imprecations. Their themes cover the whole of human experience before God: the joy of the law, the kingship of God, the Davidic king, suffering and deliverance, sin and forgiveness, God’s covenant love (hesed), worship in Zion, and the nations’ praise. Psalms 1 and 2 form a gateway to the book. Psalm 1 describes the righteous man who delights in God’s law, and Psalm 2 describes the King whom the nations rage against but whom God installs.

Where Psalms Stands in the Covenant Story

The Psalter’s structure itself tells covenant history. Books 1–2 center on David. Book 3 ends with Psalm 89, a lament that God seems to have renounced his covenant with David. Book 4 opens with Moses (Psalm 90) and answers that “the LORD reigneth” (Psalms 93, 96–99). Book 5 ends in a crescendo of hallelujahs. The covenant with David seemed broken in exile, but God’s kingship was never in doubt, and the promise would be kept.

How the Psalms Lead Us to Christ

  • Jesus’ own claim: The risen Christ said that everything “written… in the psalms, concerning me” must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44, KJV). The Psalms are among the books most frequently quoted in the New Testament.
  • Direct messianic fulfillment: Psalm 2:7 (“Thou art my Son”) is applied to Jesus at his baptism, his resurrection, and his exaltation (Mark 1:11; Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5). Psalm 110:1 is the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New Testament. Jesus used it to show that David’s son is David’s Lord (Matthew 22:41–45), and Hebrews builds on 110:4 to present Christ’s eternal priesthood (Hebrews 5–7).
  • Typological fulfillment in the suffering king: Psalm 22 begins with the cry Jesus spoke from the cross (Matthew 27:46). It also describes mocking, pierced hands and feet, and garments divided by lot (22:7–8, 16–18; John 19:24). David wrote from his own suffering, but his words were shaped by the Spirit to fit the greater Son exactly. The psalm ends in worldwide worship (22:27–31), as the gospel goes to the nations.
  • Christ as singer: Hebrews 2:12 puts Psalm 22:22 on Jesus’ lips: “in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee” (KJV). Christ is not only the subject of the Psalms but their leading singer. Augustine famously heard in them the voice of the “whole Christ,” head and body. Many Reformed preachers have adopted this cautiously, reading the Psalms first as Christ’s prayers and then as ours in him.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin called the Psalms “An Anatomy of all the Parts of the Soul,” because there is no emotion that is not represented there “as in a mirror” (Preface to his Commentary on the Psalms, 1557). The Reformed churches sang the Psalms (the Genevan Psalter, Scottish metrical psalms). Some Reformed churches still sing only Psalms (exclusive psalmody), while most, including those associated with Frame, Grudem, Packer, and Wilson, sing Psalms alongside hymns. Doug Wilson’s church is known for vigorous psalm-singing. The imprecatory psalms are hard. Reformed interpreters generally read them as cries for God’s justice against unrepentant evil, left in God’s hands (Romans 12:19), and ultimately fulfilled when Christ judges the world.

For Today

The Psalms give you words when you have none. Pray a psalm aloud today. Let Psalm 1 show you the blessed man you are not, and the Blessed Man who is your righteousness. Let Psalm 2 remind you who is really on the throne when the nations rage. Let Psalm 22 bring you to the cross, where the Son was forsaken so that you never will be.

Reflect

  1. Which psalm best expresses your heart today, and how does reading it as Christ’s prayer change how you pray it?
  2. How does Psalm 2 reshape your fears about world events and politics?

Pray

LORD, you have set your King on your holy hill. Thank you for Jesus, your Son, the Blessed Man, who was forsaken on the cross so that I might be accepted, and who now reigns as Priest forever. Teach me to pray your Psalms with him and in him. Turn my laments into praise. Let everything that has breath praise the LORD. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you… But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”
family.context: Jesus warns against turning generosity into a show. The danger is not being seen accidentally; it is craving applause. The Father sees what never trends and values quiet faithfulness. Public applause is a fragile reward. Jesus trains disciples to prefer the Father’s unseen gaze. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus often withdrew, refused manipulative spectacle, and gave himself without marketing his sacrifice. He frees us from performing spirituality. Our reward is the Father’s pleasure, secured for us in the Son who already pleased him. His own ministry often slipped away from crowds; the cross itself was obedience unto the Father more than performance for spectators. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Do one kindness this week that no one needs to know about—except God. Let secrecy train your heart away from image management. Secrecy here is freedom—freedom from managing how spiritual you look. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: Where do we feel pressure to look spiritual or impressive, and how could secrecy free us?
family.prayer: Father, you see in secret. Through Jesus, purify our motives. Teach us to give and serve for your eyes alone. Amen.

devo.title: The Fear of the LORD and the Wisdom of God
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Proverbs 1:1–7 — The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge
  2. Proverbs 3:5–12 — Trust in the LORD with all your heart
  3. Proverbs 8:22–36 — Wisdom present at creation, calling to all
  4. Proverbs 9:1–6, 13–18 — Two banquets: Lady Wisdom and Folly

New Testament fulfillment: 1 Corinthians 1:24, 30; Colossians 2:2–3

The Book and Its Themes

Proverbs is a father’s instruction to his son, gathered mostly from Solomon (1:1; 10:1; 25:1) with additions from others (chapters 30–31). Chapters 1–9 are extended speeches calling the young person to choose Wisdom over Folly, both personified as women inviting passers-by to their houses. Chapters 10–29 are short, memorable sayings on speech, work, money, family, friendship, anger, sex, justice, and power. Chapter 31 closes with the acrostic poem of the excellent wife. The theme is announced at the start: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7, KJV). Wisdom in Proverbs is not cleverness. It is skill in living rightly in God’s world, rooted in reverent relationship with him.

Where Proverbs Stands in the Covenant Story

Proverbs uses the covenant name, the LORD (Yahweh), throughout. Its wisdom is not generic self-help but life under the covenant Lord. Proverbs also roots wisdom in creation. The world is made by wisdom (3:19), so living wisely means living with the grain of God’s design. Proverbs are generally true patterns, not unconditional promises. “Train up a child in the way he should go” (22:6) describes the normal fruit of godly nurture. It is not a guarantee that overrides God’s sovereignty or a child’s responsibility. Job and Ecclesiastes stand beside Proverbs in the canon as reminders that life is not always tidy.

How Proverbs Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct apostolic claim: Christ is “the power of God, and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24, KJV), “made unto us wisdom” (1:30), the one “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).
  • Thematic analogy and careful typology in Proverbs 8: Wisdom personified in Proverbs 8 was present at creation, rejoicing before God (8:27–31). The New Testament presents Christ as the one through whom all things were made (John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:15–17; Hebrews 1:2–3), using language that echoes this chapter. Be careful here, though. In the fourth century, Arius used 8:22 (“The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way”) to argue that the Son was created. Orthodox teachers responded that Proverbs 8 is poetic personification. Its language finds fulfillment in the eternal Son, but it should not be read as a literal statement about his origin. Christ is the eternal Word, not a creature.
  • Typology of the son and the king: The ideal son who heeds his father’s instruction and the righteous king of Proverbs (for example, 16:12; 25:5; 29:14) find their perfect embodiment in Jesus. He “increased in wisdom” (Luke 2:52), always did the Father’s will, and rules justly.
  • Two banquets: Wisdom sets a table and invites the simple (9:1–6). Jesus spreads a feast and invites the poor, the crippled, and the blind (Luke 14:15–24), and he gives his own flesh and blood as true food and drink (John 6:53–58).

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin’s Institutes opens with the claim that true wisdom consists almost entirely of two parts: knowledge of God and knowledge of ourselves (Institutes 1.1.1). That is a Proverbs-shaped instinct. John Frame’s emphasis that all knowledge is under God’s lordship (The Doctrine of the Knowledge of God, 1987) is a modern Reformed restatement of Proverbs 1:7. There is no neutral knowledge. J. I. Packer’s Knowing God similarly insists that knowing about God must become knowing God. Doug Wilson’s writings on family, education, and work (for example, his classical Christian education work, Recovering the Lost Tools of Learning, 1991) express a Proverbs-like concern that wisdom be passed from fathers to children.

For Today

Wisdom is not first a technique. It is a person to fear, trust, and follow. Before you make decisions today, about your words, your money, your relationships, or your work, acknowledge him in all your ways (3:6). Read one chapter of Proverbs a day (there are thirty-one), and ask how Christ, the Wisdom of God, embodies and gives what it describes.

Reflect

  1. In which area of practical life do you most need to “lean not unto thine own understanding” today?
  2. How does seeing Christ as God’s Wisdom change Proverbs from a rulebook into an invitation?

Pray

LORD, the fear of you is the beginning of wisdom. Forgive me for leaning on my own understanding. Thank you that Christ is made my wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. Teach me to walk in his ways in my speech, my work, my money, and my home. Let me hear Wisdom’s call and come to the feast you have prepared. Amen.

family.scriptureText: “And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors… For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.”
family.context: In the Lord’s Prayer, Jesus ties our plea for forgiveness to a lifestyle of forgiving. He is not teaching that we earn pardon by being nice; he is exposing that a heart clenched against others cannot open to receive mercy. Forgiveness is a gospel mirror: receiving mercy while refusing to give it reveals a tragic inconsistency. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: We forgive because Jesus first canceled our unpayable debt at the cross. Holding grudges denies the gospel we claim. Forgiveness does not pretend harm was nothing; it releases the right to revenge into his just hands. Jesus cancels debt at infinite cost; that cost dignifies forgiveness as serious grace, not denial of harm. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Name a small offense you are still reheating. Ask Jesus for power to release it—perhaps by speaking forgiveness aloud, or by stopping the mental replay. If the wound is deep, begin with willingness and ask Jesus for help—do not fake a finished feeling. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: Is there a debt of hurt we keep collecting on, and what would it look like to cancel it as people forgiven by Jesus?
family.prayer: Father, forgive us our debts through Jesus. Soften our grip on others’ failures. Make us a forgiving household. Amen.

devo.title: Vapor Under the Sun, Hope Beyond It
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Ecclesiastes 1:1–11 — “Vanity of vanities; all is vanity”
  2. Ecclesiastes 3:1–15 — A time for everything; eternity in the heart
  3. Ecclesiastes 9:7–10 — Eat your bread with joy
  4. Ecclesiastes 12:9–14 — Fear God and keep his commandments

New Testament fulfillment: Romans 8:18–25; 1 Corinthians 15:54–58

The Book and Its Themes

Ecclesiastes is the honest journal of “the Preacher” (Qoheleth). He tests every avenue of meaning “under the sun”: wisdom, pleasure, work, wealth, and achievement. His verdict is hebel, often translated “vanity” but literally “vapor” or “breath.” Life is fleeting, elusive, and impossible to master. The wise and the fool both die (2:16). Injustice persists (4:1). Work is forgotten (2:18–21). Yet woven through the book is a counter-melody. Food, drink, work, and marriage are gifts from God to be enjoyed (2:24–26; 9:7–9). God “hath set the world [eternity] in their heart” (3:11, KJV). The conclusion is “Fear God, and keep his commandments… For God shall bring every work into judgment” (12:13–14, KJV). The themes are the limits of human understanding, death as the great leveler, the gift of ordinary joys, and the fear of God.

Where Ecclesiastes Stands in the Covenant Story

Ecclesiastes reflects life in a world under the curse of Genesis 3. Thorns, toil, and dust are the background of every chapter (compare 3:20 and Genesis 3:19). Paul says that creation was “made subject to vanity” (Romans 8:20). The Greek word he uses, mataiotēs, is the same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the hebel of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher describes the world honestly, as fallen creation waiting for redemption. He cannot see beyond the sun, but he knows that God will judge and that God’s work “shall be for ever” (3:14).

How Ecclesiastes Leads Us to Christ

  • Thematic fulfillment (vanity answered): Romans 8:18–25 explains why everything feels like vapor. Creation was subjected to futility “in hope.” Christ’s resurrection is the firstfruits of a world set free. Because of the empty tomb, Paul can say what the Preacher could not: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58, KJV).
  • Death defeated: The Preacher saw death as the end that swallows all (9:5, 10). Christ entered death and “swallowed up” death in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54). He did not deny Ecclesiastes’ realism. He answered it.
  • Thematic analogy (the one Shepherd): “The words of the wise… are given from one shepherd” (12:11, KJV). The verse refers to God as the source of wisdom. Christians rightly hear in it an echo of the Good Shepherd, through whom God speaks finally (Hebrews 1:1–2), but this is an echo, not a direct prophecy.
  • Christ as the Wise Man of the curse: Jesus lived under the sun, toiled, wept, and died. He is the Son of David who took the full weight of a cursed world on himself, so that life lived in him has eternal meaning.

Through Reformed Eyes

Calvin’s teaching on “meditation on the future life” (Institutes 3.9) and on the right use of earthly gifts (3.10) is a mature Reformed reading of Ecclesiastes. The world’s fleeting nature should loosen our grip, but God’s gifts are given for both necessity and delight. Calvin explicitly rejected an “inhuman philosophy” that permits only the bare use of creation (3.10.3). Doug Wilson, in a number of his books, emphasizes joyful enjoyment of food, drink, and ordinary pleasures as gifts from God. That strand echoes Ecclesiastes 9:7. Reformed thinkers differ on emphasis and tone, but all agree with the Preacher that the gifts are good only when received from the Giver in the fear of God.

For Today

You cannot control time, master meaning, or secure your legacy. Ecclesiastes frees you from trying. Receive today as a gift: your bread, your work, and the people you love. Do your work “with thy might” (9:10), not because it earns your significance, but because in Christ it is not in vain. Hold everything with open hands, and hold on to the risen Lord.

Reflect

  1. Where are you chasing the wind, trying to find under the sun what only God can give?
  2. What ordinary gift today can you receive with joy, giving thanks to God?

Pray

Eternal God, you have set eternity in my heart, and nothing under the sun can satisfy it. Forgive me for chasing the wind. Thank you that Christ has risen and that my labor in him is not in vain. Teach me to fear you, keep your commandments, and enjoy your gifts with a thankful heart. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Therefore do not be anxious, saying, “What shall we eat?” or “What shall we drink?” or “What shall we wear?” For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.
family.context: Jesus addresses everyday survival worries. He does not scold need; he reorders pursuit. The Father already knows. Anxiety shrinks when the kingdom—God’s reign and right ways—takes first place. Anxiety often hijacks first place by sounding responsible. Jesus reframes responsibility as seeking the Father’s reign first. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the King whose kingdom we seek. He lived without grasping, trusted the Father, and provides righteousness as a gift to all who belong to him. Seeking first means trusting his rule more than our backup plans. He is the King who knows your needs; seeking his kingdom is trusting his character more than your forecasts. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: List tonight’s top three worries. Then ask: what would seeking Jesus’ kingdom first look like in each—generosity instead of hoarding attention, prayer instead of spiraling, honesty instead of control. Reorder one decision this week—calendar, spending, or conflict—by asking what honors Jesus’ reign. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What usually gets “first” in our home when stress rises, and how can we put Jesus’ kingdom ahead of that?
family.prayer: King Jesus, our Father knows what we need. Reorder our seeking. We want your kingdom and righteousness first—trusting you with the rest. Amen.

devo.title: Love Strong as Death
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Song of Songs 1:1–4 — “Let him kiss me”: the longing of love
  2. Song of Songs 2:8–17 — The beloved comes: “Rise up, my love… and come away”
  3. Song of Songs 4:9–16 — “Thou hast ravished my heart”
  4. Song of Songs 8:6–7 — “Love is strong as death… many waters cannot quench love”

New Testament fulfillment: Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:6–9

The Book and Its Themes

The Song of Songs (“the most excellent song”) is a collection of love poetry between a bride and her beloved, associated with Solomon. It celebrates romantic and sexual love within the covenant of marriage, frankly and beautifully, with images of gardens, vineyards, spices, and springs. Its themes include the goodness of desire as God created it, mutual delight (“My beloved is mine, and I am his,” 2:16, KJV), the patience of love (“stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please,” 2:7; 3:5; 8:4, KJV), the pain of absence and the joy of reunion, and love’s exclusive, unquenchable strength (8:6–7). Some scholars find a single storyline in it, while others see a cycle of poems.

Where the Song Stands in the Covenant Story

The Song returns us to Eden. Man and woman were “naked… and were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25), and the Song’s garden imagery deliberately echoes the first garden. In a world of broken relationships (Genesis 3:16), the Song shows love restored. Marriage itself is a covenant (Malachi 2:14; Proverbs 2:17), and throughout Scripture God uses marriage to describe his covenant with his people (Isaiah 54:5; Jeremiah 2:2; Hosea 2:19–20). The Song therefore belongs in a covenantal canon on two levels. It honors human marriage, and it sings in the same key as God’s love for his bride.

How the Song Leads Us to Christ

Here especially, it helps to distinguish levels of interpretation.

  • Primary meaning: The Song is about real human love in marriage. Reading it this way is not unspiritual. It honors the Creator who made bodies and desire good.
  • Thematic fulfillment (marriage as a picture): Paul says that marriage was always a “great mystery” that speaks “concerning Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32, KJV). Every faithful marriage, including the one in the Song, is a living picture of Christ’s love. He gave himself for his bride to make her lovely (5:25–27), and history ends with “the marriage of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:7).
  • Historic Christian reading: For most of church history, including Bernard of Clairvaux, many Puritans, and many Reformed preachers, the Song has also been read as an allegory of Christ and the soul or the church. That reading can be devotionally rich. Its weakness comes when every detail is given a coded meaning the text doesn’t support. A balanced Reformed approach reads the Song first as marital poetry and then, guided by Ephesians 5, lets it deepen our wonder at Christ’s love, without forcing allegory.
  • Love strong as death: 8:6–7 finds its ultimate expression in the One whose love went into death and was not quenched by the “many waters” of judgment (compare Psalm 69:1–2; Romans 8:35–39).

Through Reformed Eyes

Reformed Christians have differed in how much weight to place on the allegorical reading. Calvin defended the book’s place in the canon when Sebastian Castellio wanted to dismiss it as merely a secular love poem. Many later Puritans preached it richly as describing Christ and the church. Modern Reformed commentators often combine both levels. Doug Wilson has written extensively on marriage and sexuality from a covenantal perspective (for example, Reforming Marriage, Canon Press, 1995), emphasizing marriage as an image of Christ and the church. Wayne Grudem’s work on biblical manhood and womanhood (for example, Recovering Biblical Manhood and Womanhood, co-edited with John Piper, 1991) also connects Ephesians 5 to God’s design for marriage. All these voices agree that the body and marital love are good gifts and that marriage points beyond itself to Christ.

For Today

If you are married, the Song invites you to cherish your spouse with delight, faithfulness, and tenderness, as a picture of Christ’s love. If you are unmarried or your marriage is hard, the Song still speaks. You are loved with a love that is “strong as death” and that many waters cannot quench. Christ rejoices over his bride (Isaiah 62:5), and that includes you.

Reflect

  1. How does the Song challenge either a prudish or a casual view of love and the body?
  2. What would change in your heart today if you truly believed Christ delights in his people as a bridegroom delights in his bride?

Pray

Lord Jesus, Bridegroom of the church, your love is better than wine, stronger than death, and unquenched by the floods of judgment. Thank you for giving yourself for your bride. Make my love faithful and pure, in marriage or in singleness. Set me as a seal upon your heart. Let me long for the marriage supper of the Lamb. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly… And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
family.context: Paul ties thankfulness to Christ’s peace ruling a shared life, and to Christ’s word dwelling richly among them. Gratitude is not a mood trick; it is the overflow of belonging to Jesus together. Thankfulness in Colossians sits next to peace ruling and the word dwelling—gratitude grows in a Christ-saturated community. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: We give thanks to the Father through Jesus—he is the mediator of every good gift and the one in whose name we live. Thanksgiving becomes Christian when it runs through him, not around him. Doing everything in Jesus’ name means his reputation and grace set the tone for ordinary words and deeds. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: Before listing blessings, name Jesus as the center of them: forgiveness, a shared table, breath, another chance. Then let that shape how you speak and act “in his name” tonight. Try ending the day by thanking the Father for one specific mercy that came through Christ. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: What is one gift we often enjoy without tracing it back to Jesus—and how can we thank the Father through him for it now?
family.prayer: Father, thank you through Jesus for your peace and your gifts. Let his word dwell in us richly, and rule our hearts with gratitude. Amen.

devo.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Servant Who Bore Our Sins
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Isaiah 6:1–8 — The vision of the holy LORD; cleansing and commission
  2. Isaiah 9:2–7 — “Unto us a child is born”
  3. Isaiah 40:1–11 — “Comfort ye my people”
  4. Isaiah 52:13–53:12 — The Suffering Servant

New Testament fulfillment: John 12:37–41; Acts 8:30–35

The Book and Its Themes

Isaiah is sometimes called “the fifth Gospel” because its vision of salvation is so rich. Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem during the eighth century BC under four kings, as Assyria threatened and the northern kingdom fell. The book moves from judgment (chapters 1–39), through comfort and the Servant’s suffering (40–55), to the glorious new creation (56–66). Its favorite title for God is “the Holy One of Israel.” Its themes are the holiness and sovereignty of God, judgment on pride and idolatry, the remnant, trust in God rather than alliances (chapters 7, 30–31), the coming Davidic King (chapters 9, 11), the Servant of the LORD (42; 49; 50; 52–53), the inclusion of the nations, and new heavens and a new earth (65:17).

Where Isaiah Stands in the Covenant Story

Isaiah confronts a covenant people who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from him (29:13). He announces exile to Babylon (39:5–7), and then, in chapters 40 onward, speaks comfort beyond exile. God promises a new exodus, a new covenant (“an everlasting covenant, even the sure mercies of David,” 55:3, KJV), and a renewed creation. The Davidic King of chapters 9 and 11 and the Servant of chapters 42–53 converge. The Servant is Israel’s representative, doing what Israel failed to do: bearing sin and bringing God’s salvation “unto the end of the earth” (49:6).

How Isaiah Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct prophecy and fulfillment: The child called “Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God” who reigns on David’s throne forever (9:6–7) is Jesus (Luke 1:32–33). The virgin’s son named Immanuel (7:14) is fulfilled in Jesus’ birth (Matthew 1:22–23). The voice in the wilderness (40:3) is John the Baptist preparing the way of the LORD, who comes in Jesus (Mark 1:2–3).
  • The Suffering Servant: When the Ethiopian official asked whom Isaiah 53 described, Philip “began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus” (Acts 8:35, KJV). The Servant “was wounded for our transgressions,” the LORD “laid on him the iniquity of us all,” he made “his soul an offering for sin,” and he will “see his seed” and “justify many” (53:5–11). That is substitutionary atonement, resurrection, and justification together. Jesus applied 53:12 to himself (Luke 22:37), and Peter quoted 53:4–9 (1 Peter 2:22–25).
  • Glory seen: John says Isaiah “saw his glory, and spake of him” (John 12:41, KJV), referring to Isaiah 6. The holy LORD on the throne was the glory of the Son.
  • New creation: Isaiah 65:17 is fulfilled in the new heavens and new earth of Revelation 21:1, inaugurated by Christ’s resurrection.

Through Reformed Eyes

Isaiah 6 is a foundational text for the Reformed vision of God’s holiness, an emphasis R. C. Sproul popularized and Packer develops in Knowing God. Isaiah 53 is central to the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution, which Packer defended and which Calvin, Frame, Grudem, and Wilson all affirm. Calvin wrote that Christ was made a substitute and surety in the place of transgressors and bore the punishment due to them (see Institutes 2.16.5–7, 10, which draws on Isaiah 53). Isaiah’s vision of nations streaming to Zion (2:2–4) is one reason for Wilson’s postmillennial optimism. Grudem’s premillennialism and amillennial readers see these texts fulfilled differently in time. All agree they will be fulfilled in Christ.

For Today

Before you are sent, you must be cleansed. Isaiah saw the Lord, said “Woe is me,” and was touched with a coal from the altar (6:5–7). Come to God today with the same honesty. Your iniquity has been laid on the Servant. Then hear the call, “Whom shall I send?”, and answer, “Here am I; send me.” Comfort others with the comfort you have received.

Reflect

  1. When did a sense of God’s holiness last bring you to “Woe is me”? What happens when you avoid that experience?
  2. Read Isaiah 53 slowly, and put your own name where it says “our” and “us.” What changes?

Pray

Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts. The whole earth is full of his glory. Woe is me, for I am a person of unclean lips. Thank you that the Servant was wounded for my transgressions and that by his stripes I am healed. Thank you that you laid my iniquity on him. Here am I; send me. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
family.context: James warns against blaming God for temptation, then pivots: God is the unchanging giver of good. The greatest gift named here is new birth by the word of truth—life from him, not self-made. James protects God’s reputation: he is not the author of evil; he is the unwavering giver of good. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: The word of truth centers on Jesus, the true light. New birth comes through the gospel of Christ by the Spirit. Every lesser gift—food, friendship, beauty—points upward to the Father who gave his Son. New birth by the word of truth is the gift that reinterprets every lesser gift—we are his firstfruits in Jesus. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Trace three good things from today back to the Father’s generosity, and thank him that the same faithful God has given you life in Jesus. Resist the deception that good things are merely luck or self-earned. Let gratitude include both bread on the table and belonging in Christ. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: Which good gift from this week most clearly reminds us of the Father’s unchanging kindness in Jesus?
family.prayer: Father of lights, every good gift comes from you. Thank you for new life through Jesus, the word of truth. Keep us undeceived and grateful. Amen.

devo.title: Broken Cisterns and the New Covenant
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Jeremiah 1:4–10 — The prophet’s call: “Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee”
  2. Jeremiah 2:11–13 — Two evils: forsaking the fountain, digging broken cisterns
  3. Jeremiah 23:5–6 — The righteous Branch: “THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS”
  4. Jeremiah 31:31–34 — The new covenant

New Testament fulfillment: Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6–13

The Book and Its Themes

Jeremiah, the “weeping prophet,” ministered for about forty years, from 627 BC through the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. He was called as a young man to “root out… pull down… build, and… plant” (1:10, KJV). He preached an unpopular message: Judah would fall to Babylon, so they should submit and wait for God’s restoration. He was beaten, imprisoned, thrown into a cistern, and called a traitor. His book includes sermons, laments (“confessions”), symbolic acts (a ruined loincloth, a smashed jar, a yoke), narratives, and oracles against the nations. Its themes are covenant unfaithfulness pictured as adultery (chapter 3), false prophets crying “Peace, peace” (6:14), the deceitful heart (17:9), God as potter (chapter 18), suffering faithfulness, the seventy years (25:11; 29:10), and the hope of restoration.

Where Jeremiah Stands in the Covenant Story

Jeremiah lived when the Mosaic covenant’s curses fell in full. Yet at the darkest moment, God gave him the brightest promise: a new covenant (31:31–34). It would not be “according to the covenant that I made with their fathers… which my covenant they brake” (31:32, KJV). God would write his law on their hearts, all would know him, and he would forgive their iniquity and “remember their sin no more.” Reformed theology understands the new covenant as the final and fullest administration of the one covenant of grace (WCF 7.6). It continues God’s promise (“I will be their God”) but surpasses the old administration in power, inwardness, scope, and finality.

How Jeremiah Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment: At the Last Supper, Jesus took the cup and said, “This cup is the new testament [covenant] in my blood” (Luke 22:20, KJV). Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34 in full, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, and declares Christ “the mediator of a better covenant” (8:6).
  • Direct messianic prophecy: The “righteous Branch” raised up for David, whose name is “THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS” (23:5–6, KJV), is Christ the King. His name points to imputed righteousness. Christ himself is our righteousness before God (1 Corinthians 1:30; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9).
  • Typology of the suffering prophet: Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem, was rejected by his own, and was treated as a criminal. Some people even thought Jesus was Jeremiah (Matthew 16:14). Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41) and was rejected by his own (John 1:11), but his suffering redeemed those who rejected him.
  • Thematic fulfillment: “The fountain of living waters” (2:13) speaks through Jesus: “If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink” (John 7:37, KJV).

Through Reformed Eyes

Jeremiah 31 is a key text in the baptism debate among the authors you appreciate. Paedobaptist Reformed theologians, such as Calvin, the Westminster tradition, Frame, and Wilson, emphasize the continuity of the covenant promise “to you and to your children” (Acts 2:39) and see the new covenant as a better administration that still includes households. Reformed Baptists, like Grudem, emphasize that in the new covenant “they shall all know me” (31:34). For them, the new covenant community properly consists of those who profess faith, so baptism is for believers. Grudem’s Systematic Theology discusses this directly in its chapter on baptism. Both sides affirm salvation by grace through faith and the new heart as God’s gift. This is a debate among brothers. The new covenant’s central promise of forgiveness and a new heart through Christ’s blood is shared by all.

For Today

Where are you digging broken cisterns, trying to draw life from things that cannot hold water? Turn back to the fountain. And rejoice in the new covenant: God has written his law on your heart, he knows you, and he remembers your sins no more. Take the Lord’s Supper this coming Lord’s Day as a covenant meal sealed with Christ’s blood.

Reflect

  1. Which “broken cistern” are you most tempted to drink from when life is hard?
  2. What does it mean to you today that God says, “I will remember their sin no more”?

Pray

Fountain of living waters, forgive me for forsaking you and digging broken cisterns. Thank you for the new covenant in Jesus’ blood. Write your law on my heart. Let me know you truly. Thank you that you remember my sins no more. Jesus, the LORD our Righteousness, clothe me in your righteousness today. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name! Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits, who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy, who satisfies you with good so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.
family.context: David talks to his own soul: do not forget. The “benefits” he lists begin with forgiveness and redemption—rescue deeper than comfort. Memory fuels worship. Self-talk matters in worship. David commands his soul to bless and remember because forgetting is easy when life is loud. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Forgiveness of iniquity and redemption from the pit find their fullness in Jesus’ cross and resurrection. He is the one who crowns us with steadfast love. Remembering benefits means remembering him. Each benefit in the psalm deepens in Jesus: forgiven, healed in hope, redeemed, crowned with covenant love. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Tell one story of God’s help in your family’s past—answered prayer, provision, reconciliation. “Forget not” is a shared practice: speak the mercies so they stay alive. Storytelling is discipleship. A remembered mercy becomes tomorrow’s faith. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: What benefit of God through Jesus do we most need to remember out loud tonight so we do not forget?
family.prayer: Lord, we bless your holy name. Through Jesus you forgive, redeem, and crown us with love. Help our souls forget not your benefits. Amen.

devo.title: Great Is Thy Faithfulness in the Ruins
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Lamentations 1:1–12 — The desolate city: “Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by?”
  2. Lamentations 3:19–33 — “His compassions fail not… great is thy faithfulness”
  3. Lamentations 3:40–58 — “Let us search and try our ways”
  4. Lamentations 5:15–22 — “Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD”

New Testament fulfillment: Luke 19:41–44; 2 Corinthians 1:3–5

The Book and Its Themes

Lamentations is five poems of grief over Jerusalem’s destruction by Babylon in 586 BC. Tradition attributes them to Jeremiah. Four of the poems are acrostics, with each verse or stanza beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapter 3 triples it. The form itself expresses grief “from A to Z,” ordered and complete. The themes are the horror of judgment (the city is like a widow, children starve, the temple is defiled), the honest acknowledgment that God is righteous and the people have sinned (1:18), raw lament addressed to God, and at the very center of the book a rising confession of hope: “It is of the LORD’S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness” (3:22–23, KJV).

Where Lamentations Stands in the Covenant Story

Lamentations is the covenant curse experienced. What Deuteronomy 28 threatened has happened. Yet Lamentations does not abandon the covenant. It appeals to it. The hope of chapter 3 rests on God’s hesed (steadfast covenant love) and his faithfulness. Even the final, unresolved prayer, “Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned” (5:21, KJV), anticipates the new-covenant gift of a heart turned by grace. Reformed theology calls this sovereign, effectual grace: God must turn us before we can turn.

How Lamentations Leads Us to Christ

  • Thematic fulfillment (the Weeper): Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold its destruction in A.D. 70 (Luke 19:41–44). He is the compassionate Lord whose heart breaks over his people’s ruin.
  • Typology of the afflicted man: Chapter 3 begins, “I am the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath” (3:1, KJV). The speaker represents the suffering community. Christian readers have long heard in this an anticipation of Christ, who bore the rod of God’s wrath, not for his own sin, but for ours (Isaiah 53:4–6). In chapter 3 the poet speaks of bitterness, wormwood, and gall (3:15, 19), and his enemies “hiss” and mock (2:15–16). These echoes resonate with the passion, but they are typological and thematic rather than explicit prophecy.
  • Devotional application of 1:12: “Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow” (KJV). Originally these are the words of Jerusalem personified. The church has long sung them on Good Friday as an echo of Christ’s sufferings. This is a fitting devotional application, but not the verse’s original meaning, and the New Testament does not quote it this way.
  • Morning mercies: The compassion that does not fail is secured at the cross. Because the full wrath fell on Christ, God’s mercy toward those in him is new every morning (Romans 8:1, 32).

Through Reformed Eyes

The Reformed tradition, sometimes caricatured as cold, has deep resources for lament. Calvin’s commentaries on Jeremiah and Lamentations treat affliction as the fatherly discipline of God for his children (compare Institutes 3.8 on bearing the cross). J. I. Packer, in Knowing God, writes about God’s goodness and his severity, and about the comfort of God’s unchanging character. That is the theology of Lamentations 3. The hymn “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” (Thomas Chisholm, 1923) brought these verses into the church’s worship.

For Today

You are allowed to lament. Scripture gives you five chapters of it. Bring your grief to God in ordered, honest words. Then, in the middle of the ruins, recall: “This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope” (3:21, KJV). The mercies of God did not run out yesterday. They are new this morning, because Christ has drunk the cup of wrath to the dregs.

Reflect

  1. What loss or grief do you need to bring to God in honest lament rather than hiding it?
  2. What specific truths about God’s character can you “recall to mind” when hope feels thin?

Pray

LORD, your compassions fail not. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness. I bring you the ruins in my life and in the world, and I confess my sin where it has contributed. Thank you that Jesus bore the rod of your wrath so that I might know only fatherly mercy. Turn me to yourself, and I will be turned. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In any and every circumstance, I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me.
family.context: Paul writes from hardship, not a spa. Contentment is learned, not automatic, and it stretches across both lack and plenty. The “secret” is not stoicism; it is Christ’s strengthening presence. Contentment that only works in comfort is not yet what Paul learned. He learned Christ in both directions. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: “Through him who strengthens me” points to Jesus as the living source of endurance. Contentment is not pretending needs vanish; it is depending on Christ’s sufficiency when circumstances swing. Strength “through him” keeps contentment from becoming pride in toughness; it is dependence on Jesus. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Name one place you feel discontent—comparison, craving more, restless scrolling. Ask Jesus for strength to receive today’s portion with trust rather than constant reaching. Practice saying “enough for today” about one craving that usually owns your mood. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: Where do we struggle most with contentment—lack or plenty—and how can Jesus’ strength meet us there?
family.prayer: Jesus, you strengthen us in every circumstance. Teach our family the secret of contentment in you, whether we have little or much. Amen.

devo.title: The Glory Departs and Returns: Hearts of Flesh and Dry Bones Alive
devo.html:
Scripture readings

  1. Ezekiel 1:26–28 — The likeness of the glory of the LORD
  2. Ezekiel 34:11–24 — “I myself will search for my sheep”; one Shepherd, my servant David
  3. Ezekiel 36:24–28 — A new heart and a new spirit
  4. Ezekiel 37:1–14 — The valley of dry bones

New Testament fulfillment: John 10:11–16; John 3:3–8

The Book and Its Themes

Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in the first deportation (597 BC). There, by the river Chebar, he saw visions of God’s glory on a throne-chariot (chapter 1). He was commissioned as a watchman (3:17; 33:7) and performed strange sign-acts: lying on his side, eating siege bread, and shaving his head. He saw the glory of the LORD depart from the defiled temple (chapters 8–11) before Jerusalem’s fall. After the fall (chapter 33) his message turned to hope: a true Shepherd, a new heart, dry bones raised, a reunited people, victory over Gog, and a visionary new temple from which a river of life flows (chapters 40–48). The book ends, “The LORD is there” (48:35, KJV). Its themes are God’s glory and holiness, the purpose that nations “shall know that I am the LORD” (repeated over 60 times), individual responsibility (chapter 18), judgment, and resurrection-renewal by the Spirit.

Where Ezekiel Stands in the Covenant Story

Ezekiel explains the exile theologically. God’s presence cannot remain amid idolatry, so the glory leaves (10:18–19; 11:22–23). But God is not finished. He promises to act “for mine holy name’s sake” (36:22). He will cleanse his people, give them a new heart and his Spirit, cause them to walk in his statutes, and be their God (36:25–28). This is the same new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31, now with explicit emphasis on the Spirit. He will make “a covenant of peace… an everlasting covenant” and set his sanctuary among them forever (37:26–27).

How Ezekiel Leads Us to Christ

  • Direct fulfillment (the Shepherd): God says, “I, even I, will both search my sheep,” and also, “I will set up one shepherd over them… my servant David” (34:11, 23, KJV). Both are fulfilled when Jesus says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). He is the LORD himself coming to seek the lost (Luke 19:10), and the Son of David ruling his flock.
  • Fulfillment by the Spirit: Jesus told Nicodemus, “Ye must be born again… of water and of the Spirit” (John 3:5–7, KJV). As “a master of Israel” (3:10), Nicodemus should have known Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises to sprinkle clean water and put his Spirit within. Regeneration is Ezekiel’s promise fulfilled in Christ’s ministry.
  • Resurrection: The dry bones (37:1–14) primarily depict the national restoration of exiled Israel (“these bones are the whole house of Israel,” 37:11). They also reveal a God who raises the dead by his word and Spirit. That anticipates both spiritual regeneration (Ephesians 2:1–5) and the bodily resurrection secured by Christ (John 5:25–29).
  • The glory and the temple: The glory that departed returns in Ezekiel’s vision (43:1–5). In the New Testament it returns in Jesus (John 1:14), dwells in the church by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16), and fills the new creation, which has no temple “for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it” (Revelation 21:22, KJV). The river of Ezekiel 47 flows again in Revelation 22:1–2.

Through Reformed Eyes

Ezekiel 36–37 is one of the clearest Old Testament pictures of what Reformed theology calls monergistic regeneration: God alone gives life to the spiritually dead (WCF 10.1–2; Calvin, Institutes 2.3.6–10; Grudem’s chapter on regeneration). Interpretation of Ezekiel 40–48 divides readers. Most confessional Reformed interpreters read the visionary temple as symbolically fulfilled in Christ, the church, and the new creation. (Calvin’s own Ezekiel lectures ended at chapter 20 when he died.) Dispensational readers expect a literal future temple. Historic premillennialists like Grudem differ from dispensationalists on many points, so don’t assume every premillennialist reads Ezekiel 40–48 the same way. All Reformed readers affirm that Christ’s sacrifice is final (Hebrews 10:12–14).

For Today

Perhaps parts of your life feel like a valley of dry bones: a cold heart, a dead relationship, a church in decline. The question is still, “Can these bones live?” The answer is still, “O Lord GOD, thou knowest” (37:3, KJV). Speak God’s word over the dry places and pray for the breath of the Spirit. The Good Shepherd is searching for his sheep, and the One who raised Jesus from the dead gives life.

Reflect

  1. Where do you most need the Spirit to give you a “heart of flesh” in place of stone?
  2. Who is a “lost sheep” you can pray for and seek in the name of the Good Shepherd this week?

Pray

Sovereign LORD, for the sake of your holy name, cleanse me from all my idols. Take away my heart of stone and give me a heart of flesh. Put your Spirit within me and cause me to walk in your ways. Good Shepherd, search for your scattered sheep. Breathe on the dry bones of your church. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, “Take this, and divide it among yourselves… And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.”
family.context: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus gave thanks over bread and cup that signified his coming death. Gratitude and sacrifice met at the same table.
