family.jesusConnection: We pray to the Father through the Son who taught us this confidence. Jesus reveals the Father’s heart and opens the way by his own mediation. Good gifts climax in the gift of himself and the Spirit. We ask through the Son who reveals the Father’s heart and secures our access. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: As the year ends, ask openly: what do we need to ask, seek, and knock for—wisdom, healing of a relationship, courage for a next step? Pray it simply together. Write the ask in one sentence and pray it without decorating it. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: What good gift from the Father are we being invited to ask for through Jesus as this year closes?
family.prayer: Father in heaven, through Jesus we ask, seek, and knock. Give good gifts according to your wisdom, and teach us to trust your heart. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
family.context: The Christian life is a race of endurance, not a sprint of vibes. Weights and clinging sin slow us. The key strategy is directional: looking to Jesus, who pioneered and completes faith and now sits enthroned. Endurance races need a focal point. Weights drop when eyes stay on Jesus. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus connects start and finish of faith. He endured the cross for joy—our redemption and his exaltation. Fixing our eyes on him means interpreting the year’s gains and losses through his finished work and present reign. He perfected faith by enduring the cross for joy; we run in his wake, not in parallel self-salvation. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Name one weight to lay aside before a new year—resentment, comparison, a habit that drains love. Then literally “look to Jesus”: read this passage again slowly as your closing focus. Lay aside the weight you named with a concrete next step—confession, deletion, apology. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: What weight or clinging sin do we need to lay aside so we can run looking to Jesus?
family.prayer: Jesus, founder and perfecter of our faith—we fix our eyes on you. You endured the cross for joy. Give us endurance and freedom to run with you. Amen.

family.scriptureText: So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom… Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days… Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!
family.context: Moses’ psalm faces human frailty honestly, then asks for wisdom that numbers days, joy rooted in steadfast love, and God’s establishing of ordinary work. Time becomes meaningful under mercy. Numbering days is wisdom, not morbidity. Moses asks for love-satisfied joy and established work. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: In Jesus, steadfast love is satisfied fully—morning mercies with a cross-shaped proof. He establishes work that seems small by joining it to his kingdom. Wisdom numbering days leads us to invest life in him. In Jesus, steadfast love has a face and established work joins kingdom purpose. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Review the year briefly without cruelty: where did you see God’s steadfast love? Offer tomorrow’s work to him to establish—school, job, home care—as kingdom-connected labor. Offer tomorrow’s ordinary labor to God as something he can establish. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: If we number our days with wisdom, what deserves more of our attention in Jesus’ name next year?
family.prayer: Lord, teach us to number our days. Satisfy us with your steadfast love in Jesus. Establish the work of our hands for your glory. Amen.

family.scriptureText: But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness. “The Lord is my portion,” says my soul, “therefore I will hope in him.”
family.context: In a book of grief, hope rises by deliberate remembering: steadfast love, endless mercies, morning renewal, great faithfulness. The soul chooses the Lord as portion when circumstances feel empty. Hope in Lamentations is remembered, not mood-based. Mercy is morning-new because God is faithful. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is the Lord’s portion made personal—Emmanuel whose mercies meet us each morning through finished redemption and living intercession. New Year hope is not optimism; it is faithfulness proven in Christ. Jesus is the portion that does not shrink when years change. New Year courage is his faithfulness. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: On New Year’s Eve, call mercy to mind out loud. Refuse both despair and self-hype. Say together: “The Lord is our portion”—and name Jesus as the reason that sentence holds. Speak “great is your faithfulness” over both regrets and hopes before midnight habits take over. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What mercy from God through Jesus do we need to call to mind so hope rises for the year ahead?
family.prayer: Faithful Lord, your mercies are new every morning. Jesus is our portion and our hope. We enter what comes next trusting your steadfast love. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Pray then like this: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.”
family.context: Jesus teaches prayer that starts with God—Father, holy name, kingdom, will—before daily bread and personal need. The year’s first posture is worship and surrender, not self-launch. Jesus’ model prayer prioritizes God’s name and will before our list. That order is mercy for anxious planners. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: We pray “Father” because Jesus brings us home as siblings with him. Kingdom and will center on the King’s agenda. Starting the year with this prayer aligns a household with Jesus’ own priorities before the Father. Because Jesus brings us to the Father, “our” Father is a shared family address for the year. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: Pray the first lines slowly as a family dedication of the year. Then ask what “your will be done” might mean in one practical arena—speech, calendar, generosity. Dedicate the year with those first lines, then attach one practical “will be done” to your calendar. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: What would it look like for God’s name to be hallowed and his will sought first in our home this year?
family.prayer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done—in our family on earth as in heaven—through Jesus our Lord. Amen.

family.scriptureText: We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.
family.context: Paul grounds ethics in union: buried with Christ, raised to walk new. Newness is not a calendar trick; it is resurrection life shared with Jesus. Death to the old self is the doorway. Baptismal union language makes newness theological: buried and raised with Christ. Read the passage slowly aloud, then sit with one phrase that stands out before anyone explains it.
family.jesusConnection: Union with Jesus’ death and resurrection is the Christian’s deepest “new year.” We walk new because we are joined to the risen Christ by the Father’s glory—not because January magic resets us. Walking new is possible because resurrection life is shared, not because willpower reinvented you on January 1. This is how we are connected to Jesus tonight: not by vague inspiration, but by his person and finished work applied to ordinary life by the Spirit.
family.application: Identify one old pattern to bury with Christ again—bitterness, secrecy, harsh humor—and one newness to practice as risen people: honesty, blessing, Sabbath rest. Name the pattern to bury and the practice to walk—then ask for the Spirit’s power. Keep the step small enough to finish before tomorrow night, and specific enough that anyone in the room could notice it happened.
family.talk: What does walking in newness of life with Jesus look like for us in January, concretely?
family.prayer: Father of glory, we are united with Christ in death and resurrection. Help us walk in newness of life together by your power. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
family.context: Paul refuses both complacency and paralysis. He presses on because Christ already seized him. The past is neither erased nor enthroned; the upward call in Christ defines direction. Paul’s press-on energy is response to being already Christ’s possession. Let the historical setting stay in view: real people, real pressures, a real God acting in time.
family.jesusConnection: Christ Jesus has made us his own—that is the engine. We pursue him because we are possessed by him. The prize is God’s upward call in Christ, not self-made achievement. Forgetting what lies behind is not amnesia; it is refusing to let the past be lord. Jesus is Lord. Union with Christ means what is true of him for us becomes the ground of how we live with each other.
family.application: Name one thing behind you to stop rehearsing, and one forward step of faithfulness in Jesus—reconciliation, a habit of Scripture, serving someone. Press on without pretending perfection. Choose one forward faithfulness and take it within three days. If emotions are tender, lower the volume and raise the honesty; Jesus is not impressed by performance.
family.talk: How does “Christ Jesus has made me his own” change the way we press on this year?
family.prayer: Christ Jesus, you have made us your own. We press on toward the upward call in you—forgetting what enslaves us behind, straining forward in grace. Amen.

family.theme: Wise and Foolish Builders at Work
family.scriptureText: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror and then goes away and at once forgets what he was like. But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.
family.context: James warns that hearing without doing is self-deception—like forgetting your face after a mirror glance. Blessing rests on persevering action shaped by the liberating word. The mirror metaphor exposes religious consumption without transformation. Notice who is speaking and who is listening in the text; that often unlocks the point for a household.
family.jesusConnection: The Word we hear is fulfilled in Jesus, and he sends the Spirit so we can act. Doing the word is life in liberty under the Lord who first acted for us—not earning love, but embodying received truth. Doing the word is liberty under Jesus, because he fulfilled the law and empowers obedience by the Spirit. We do not use Jesus as a mascot for family values; we belong to him, and that belonging reshapes our values.
family.application: Pick one truth from this 60-day journey you have heard and not yet practiced. Do it in the next 48 hours. Let the mirror become a path. Convert one heard truth from this series into a 48-hour action. Invite each person to own one phrase from the reading as their takeaway, then pray that phrase back to God.
family.talk: What word from Jesus are we in danger of hearing only—and what is one doing step we will take?
family.prayer: Lord Jesus, free us from hearing-only faith. Make us doers of your word who persevere, blessed in the doing by your grace. Amen.

family.scriptureText: Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.”… And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh.
family.context: Foreign sages travel far to find a child-king. They ask, journey, rejoice, fall down, and give. Worship is costly seeking that ends in glad surrender of treasure. Epiphany wise men show that seeking Jesus may cross cultures and cost treasure. Scripture here is not a slogan for the fridge only; it is a window into God’s heart toward us.
family.jesusConnection: Jesus is King of the Jews and Lord of the nations—worthy of Gentile worship from the start. Epiphany reveals him to outsiders. We connect to Jesus the way they did: seek, bow, give him our best. Falling down to worship a child declares his kingship; gifts answer his worth. His life, teaching, cross, and resurrection are the source; our response is trust that shows up in practice.
family.application: Offer Jesus a “treasure” tomorrow: time, praise, resources, or a skill used for someone’s good. Let January begin with worship gifts, not only resolutions. Decide the treasure you will open for him this week and follow through. End by thanking Jesus out loud for one concrete mercy from today so application stays relational, not mechanical.
family.talk: What treasure can we open for Jesus—the born King—as this season of revealing continues?
family.prayer: Born King Jesus, like the wise men we seek you and worship you. Receive the treasures of our hearts and hands. Lead us by your light. Amen.

family.scriptureText: And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
family.context: The risen Jesus claims total authority, then sends his people on a disciple-making mission with a Trinitarian baptismal name and a teaching task—and promises his presence to the age’s end. The Great Commission rests on Jesus’ all-authority and ends with his always-presence—courage with company. If the day has been loud, let this reading be the first quiet truth that gets a full hearing.
family.jesusConnection: Our sixty days end where Christian life always aims: under Jesus’ authority, with Jesus’ mission, in Jesus’ presence. He connects heaven’s authority to earth’s going. We are never sent alone. Making disciples is the natural overflow of sixty days spent knowing him: baptizing belonging, teaching obedience. The Spirit takes what is Christ’s and makes it vivid among us—comfort, conviction, courage, and love.
family.application: Ask how your household can take one disciple-making step: pray for someone far from Jesus, share what you have learned, invite, serve, or encourage baptismal faithfulness in your church family. Pick one relational next step—pray, invite, share, encourage—and treat his “I am with you” as enough. Write the talk question somewhere visible until it is answered; unfinished conversations can still be holy.
family.talk: As Jesus sends us with “I am with you always,” what is one next step of making disciples we can take together?
family.prayer: Risen Jesus, all authority is yours. Send our family under your word. Teach us to make disciples, and keep your promise—be with us always. Amen.
